name: Platform as a service (PaaS)
summary: You hand the platform your code or a container image, and it builds it, runs it as a set of long-lived processes, routes requests to them, restarts them when they fail and scales them, so you never manage servers or an operating system.
howItWorks: You push source code, usually with `git push`, plus a short declaration of what to run: on Heroku and Dokku a `Procfile` with lines such as `web: java -jar lib/foobar.jar $PORT`. A build step turns the code into something runnable. Buildpacks do this without a Dockerfile: each one runs `detect` (a Python buildpack looks for `requirements.txt`, a Node.js one for a lockfile) and then `build`, which downloads dependencies, compiles the code and sets the start command. The result is a slug (a tarball of the app and its runtime) or, with Cloud Native Buildpacks, an OCI container image. The platform combines that build with the app’s config, which it injects as environment variables, into a numbered, append-only release, so rolling back means starting an older release. It then starts the release as processes on its own machines: Heroku calls them dynos, Cloud Foundry app instances on Diego cells. You scale by setting a count per process type (`web=3 worker=2`), or let an autoscaler do it. A router owns the public hostname and spreads incoming HTTP requests over the healthy `web` processes; Heroku’s routers pick a dyno at random. A process manager restarts crashed processes, moves them off failing hardware and replaces all of them on every deploy. Because any process can be killed and replaced, local disk is ephemeral: anything worth keeping lives in an attached backing service, such as a database whose URL arrives in `DATABASE_URL`. This is the contract the twelve-factor app methodology, written at Heroku, spells out.
analogy: A serviced office instead of a building. You bring your team and your work; the landlord runs the reception desk that sends visitors to a free desk, the cleaning, the heating and the repairs, and adds desks when you grow. You can’t knock down walls or keep things on a desk overnight, because the desk you get tomorrow may be a different one, so anything important goes in the filing room down the hall.
useWhen: A web app or API with ordinary needs: HTTP in, a database and a cache out, a background worker or two
A small team that would rather not patch operating systems, configure load balancers or run Kubernetes
You want deploys to be one `git push` or one CLI command, with releases you can roll back
The app already follows the twelve-factor rules: config in environment variables, no state on local disk
avoidWhen: The app needs local state that must survive a restart, such as files written to disk: every Heroku dyno gets a fresh filesystem and loses its writes when it stops or restarts
Requests run long: Heroku’s router ends any request that takes more than 30 seconds, and the limit can’t be changed, so long work belongs in a worker or a queue
You need control below the app: kernel settings, special hardware, unusual networking or a sidecar per process. Use VMs or container orchestration instead
Traffic is rare and bursty and you only want to pay per request: serverless functions scale to zero by design, while most PaaS processes are always on
example: A team runs a Python web app with a background worker. Its `Procfile` has two lines, `web` and `worker`, and a `git push heroku main` sends the code to Heroku. The Python buildpack detects `requirements.txt`, runs `pip install` and produces a build, and Heroku pairs it with the config vars as release v1. The team runs `heroku ps:scale web=3 worker=1` on Standard-1X dynos (0.5 GB each, $25 a month per dyno on the Common Runtime), so $100 a month for compute. A Postgres add-on sets `DATABASE_URL` and a Key-Value Store add-on sets `REDIS_URL`; the code reads both from the environment. Heroku’s routers send each request to one of the 3 web dynos at random. Report exports took 2 minutes and kept failing with the router’s 30-second timeout, so the web dyno now pushes them onto the Redis queue and the worker builds them. Each deploy creates a new release and replaces every dyno; one bad deploy was undone with `heroku releases:rollback`.

providers.aws: AWS Elastic Beanstalk (Standard mode runs apps on EC2, Cluster mode on EKS; no charge beyond the resources it creates); AWS App Runner (source code or an image to a scaling web service; closed to new customers, and AWS points new users to Amazon ECS Express Mode)
providers.gcp: App Engine (services, versions and instances scaled on demand; Google now recommends Cloud Run for new apps); Cloud Run (stateless container instances that scale on requests; `gcloud run deploy --source` builds the image with Google Cloud’s buildpacks)
providers.azure: Azure App Service (.NET, Java, Node.js, Python and PHP on Windows or Linux, or a custom container); Azure Container Apps (serverless containers that scale on HTTP traffic, events, CPU or memory, or any KEDA scaler)
providers.oss: Cloud Foundry (`cf push`, buildpacks, Diego); Dokku (a single-host “mini-Heroku” built on Docker, MIT); Coolify (self-hostable, Apache 2.0); CapRover (Docker and nginx); hosted: Heroku (Salesforce), Render, Railway, Koyeb, Fly.io; FlashPanel sets up servers you rent elsewhere

source: # Procfile at the repository root: one process type per line
git push heroku main                      # build with a buildpack, create a release, start dynos
heroku ps:scale web=3 queue=2             # three web processes behind the router, two workers
heroku config:set ENCRYPTION_KEY=secret   # new release; the app reads it from ENV
heroku addons:create heroku-redis:mini    # attach a backing service; REDIS_URL is set for you
heroku releases:rollback v102             # start an earlier build and config again

diagram.caption: Requests reach the platform’s router, which spreads them over a pool of identical app instances. A burst makes the platform start more instances (amber while they boot); when it passes, the extra instances are stopped and two stay running. Every instance talks to the same attached database, because none of them keeps data on its own disk.

sections.title: Where PaaS sits
sections.intro: The service models differ in what you hand over and what the provider runs for you. PaaS sits between renting machines or containers and handing over single functions.

rows.label: Virtual machines (IaaS)
values: A machine image and everything inside it
You add machines, or configure an autoscaling group

rows.label: Containers and orchestration
values: Container images plus a description of how to run them
The cluster, if it is a managed service
Replica counts and autoscalers you configure

rows.label: Platform as a service
values: Source code (or an image) and a list of process types
The build, the OS, the router, restarts, logs and scaling
A count per process type, or an autoscaler

rows.label: Functions (FaaS)
values: One function per event or request
Everything, including when an instance exists at all

notes: The lines blur. Cloud Run and Azure Container Apps take a container image but run it the PaaS way, with routing and request-based scaling built in. Heroku’s Fir generation and Elastic Beanstalk’s Cluster mode run on Kubernetes underneath, and Heroku’s Eco dynos sleep after 30 minutes without traffic, like a function scaled to zero.

sections.title: Long-running processes, not functions
body: A PaaS runs your app the way you would run it on your laptop: a process starts, binds to the port in `$PORT` and serves request after request until it is stopped. One web process can hold connections open, keep a warm in-memory cache and use a connection pool. You pay for each process while it runs, whether it is busy or not: Heroku lists dynos from $7 a month (Basic) to $1,500 a month (Performance-2XL) and bills them by usage.

Serverless functions turn that around. The platform starts an instance when an event arrives, may run one request per instance, and removes idle instances, so you pay per invocation and nothing when idle, at the cost of cold starts and limits on run time. If your app is a normal web server, a PaaS fits it without changes; if it is a handful of handlers that run now and then, functions are cheaper.

sections.title: The twelve-factor contract
sections.intro: The twelve-factor app, written by Heroku co-founder Adam Wiggins in 2011, lists what an app must do so that a platform can run it without knowing anything about it. These five factors carry most of the weight.

items.name: Config in the environment
items.text: Database URLs, credentials and hostnames live in environment variables, not in the code or in per-environment config files. The test: could the code be open-sourced at any moment without leaking a credential?

items.name: Backing services as attached resources
items.text: A database, a queue or an SMTP server is a resource reached through a URL in the config. Swapping a local MySQL for Amazon RDS, or a failing database for a restored copy, changes the config and not the code.

items.name: Stateless processes
items.text: Memory and local disk are only a scratchpad for one request or job. A restart, a deploy or a move to another machine wipes them, and the next request may land on a different process anyway, so sticky sessions are out.

items.name: Port binding
items.text: The app brings its own web server library and listens on a port. The platform’s routing layer maps the public hostname to those ports.

items.name: Disposability
items.text: Processes start in seconds and shut down cleanly on `SIGTERM`: web processes stop accepting requests and finish the current ones, workers return their job to the queue. That is what lets the platform scale, deploy and move them at any moment.

sections.title: PaaS in 2026
body: The idea won, but several of the original platforms are now in maintenance. On February 6, 2026, Heroku moved to a “sustaining engineering model focused on stability, security, reliability, and support” and stopped offering Enterprise Account contracts to new customers; it still ships smaller features such as 1 GB slugs and Heroku Postgres Advanced. AWS closed App Runner to new customers, keeping it running for existing ones without new features, and recommends Amazon ECS Express Mode instead. Google’s own App Engine overview recommends Cloud Run to new users.

Meanwhile the parts PaaS invented became standards. Cloud Native Buildpacks, started by Pivotal and Heroku in 2018, graduated in the CNCF on August 11, 2026, and turn source code into an OCI image that any container platform can run. Heroku’s Fir generation runs dynos on Kubernetes (Amazon EKS), Elastic Beanstalk added a Cluster mode on EKS, and an SAP team showed an unchanged Cloud Foundry running on any Kubernetes cluster. The developer experience stays: push code, get a URL.

groups.name: Hosted platforms
groups.summary: Push code or an image and the company runs it on its own infrastructure.

groups.name: On your own servers
groups.summary: The platform layer runs on machines you rent or own.

story: Before PaaS, putting a web app online meant running the infrastructure stack yourself: servers or virtual machines, the software on them, deploys and scaling. Heroku, founded in 2007 by James Lindenbaum, Adam Wiggins and Orion Henry, started as a place to run Ruby apps where none of that was your job. When Salesforce agreed to buy it in December 2010 for about $212 million, its press release summed up the pitch: “there are no virtual machines to manage, no software to install, and no hardware to manage and tune.” Heroku then ran more than 105,000 apps.

Others arrived quickly. Google launched a preview of App Engine on April 7, 2008, for the first 10,000 developers: web apps on Google’s infrastructure, with storage built on Bigtable and GFS, automatic scaling and load balancing. On April 12, 2011, VMware released Cloud Foundry as an open-source PaaS: the code went on GitHub under Apache 2.0, and VMware said it was built to be “multi-cloud”, working across private and public environments. The same year, Heroku conceived buildpacks, the scripts that turn source code into a runnable build, and Wiggins wrote down the lessons from hundreds of thousands of Heroku apps as the twelve-factor app.

Containers then changed what a platform builds and runs. In 2018 Pivotal and Heroku started Cloud Native Buildpacks, which produce standard OCI images instead of platform-specific slugs, and it graduated in the CNCF in 2026. Heroku ended its free plans in November 2022, citing fraud and abuse. By 2026 the big platforms were consolidating: Heroku moved to sustaining engineering, AWS closed App Runner to new customers and Google pointed App Engine users to Cloud Run, while the model itself lives on in container platforms that build from source and route requests for you.

choices.choice: Build from source with buildpacks, not from a machine image or a Dockerfile
choices.why: Each buildpack detects its language from files such as `requirements.txt` and knows how to install dependencies and compile, so developers only push code. Cloud Native Buildpacks say the same knowledge then sits with one specialized team instead of in every project’s Dockerfile.

Twelve-factor picked env vars because they are easy to change between deploys without changing code, unlikely to be checked into the repository by mistake, and a language- and OS-agnostic standard, unlike config files or Java system properties.

choices.choice: Stateless processes with an ephemeral filesystem
choices.why: If no process holds data that matters, the platform can restart one daily, replace all of them on a deploy, move them off failing hardware or add more at any moment. Twelve-factor notes that a restart usually wipes local memory and disk anyway.

choices.choice: Backing services attached through a URL
choices.why: Treating a database or a mail server as an attached resource, located by a URL in the config, lets a platform provision it as an add-on or a service binding and hand it to the app, and lets operators swap it without touching code.
